q: I build everything with AI and can't write code. Am I a programmer?
alt: Do I need to learn to code?
a: Yes, you are already programming. You decide what should exist, the input, the rule and the output, and you steer the agent until it's right. Drake puts it this way: programming and engineering are different from coding, and nobody needs to know how to write the letters. The next step isn't typing code, it's learning to *know* your result is right. That's what this track teaches, starting with `sh examples/start-01-you-already-program/run.sh`.

q: What does engineering add to vibe coding?
a: One habit, mostly: saying how you'll know you got it. Before the agent runs anything, write down what the right answer is for an input you chose, then compare. Add looking at what actually changed and asking for evidence, and you're engineering. None of it needs you to write code by hand.

q: Why did the compiler refuse my program instead of just running it?
a: Because the computer never guesses what you meant. In lesson 1, `c = 0` was refused with error 11: the compiler couldn't tell what kind of number 0 was meant to be. A refusal is the computer asking you to be precise before anything runs. That's much better than quietly picking for you and being wrong later.

q: What is an exit code?
alt: What is rc in the output?
a: A number every program hands back when it finishes. `rc=0` usually means it went fine; any other number says what went wrong. Drake's examples always print it, so you can see how each run ended without guessing.

q: How do I test what my AI agent built if I can't read code?
alt: How do I check an agent's work?
a: Write down the expected answer before you run it, then compare it exactly with what you observe: MATCH or MISMATCH. Choose inputs that could trip it up (two spaces, empty input, several lines), not just the easy one. You don't need to read the code to pick good inputs. Try `sh examples/start-02-your-first-check/run.sh`.

q: My agent says all tests pass. Is that enough?
alt: All tests passed, am I done?
a: Ask what the tests compare, and whether they've ever failed. In lesson 2 a check that only asks 'did it exit 0?' passes a word counter that's wrong on three of four inputs. A check that can't fail isn't checking anything.

q: What is a negative control?
alt: Why test something that's wrong on purpose?
a: Something you know is wrong, which your check must reject. If the check accepts it, the check is broken. In lesson 2 the buggy word counter is the negative control: the real check rejected it, the weak 'did it run' check didn't.

q: Why write the expected answer before running?
alt: Why not just look at the output?
a: Because once you've seen the output, it's very easy to talk yourself into believing it's right. Writing the answer first makes the comparison honest.

q: How do I see what my agent actually changed?
alt: What did the AI change in my project?
How to read a git diff
a: Use git. `git diff --stat` lists every changed file and how many lines changed; `git diff` shows the exact lines, `-` removed and `+` added. For each file ask: did I ask for this? Read the full diff for anything you didn't. Try `sh examples/start-03-reading-the-diff/run.sh`.

q: My agent changed files I didn't ask about. What should I do?
a: Don't accept them on trust. Read that part of the diff, then send it back: 'Only change what I asked for. If you think this should change, tell me why and I'll decide.' In lesson 3 an agent asked to fix a typo also raised an upload limit from 10 to 100 and deleted the test that would have caught it.

q: Why is a deleted test a red flag?
alt: Is it ok if the agent removes tests?
a: A test is a protection you were counting on. Deleting one can hide another change, like a raised limit. Always read a deleted test before you accept a change.

q: What are git, a commit and a branch?
a: git keeps the full history of a folder so every change can be seen and undone. A commit is one saved step in that history. A branch is a separate line of work, so an agent can try things without touching the main version. A diff is the exact difference between two versions.

q: My agent says it's done. How do I know?
alt: How do I verify an AI's claim?
a: Ask which of four words it really is, and for the evidence that goes with it: PROPOSED (a plan, no evidence needed), IMPLEMENTED (a commit), EXERCISED (the exact command and its real output), QUALIFIED (the project's official check, its gate, printed PASS). Try `sh examples/start-04-asking-for-evidence/run.sh`.

q: What does NOT_RUN mean?
alt: The check was skipped, is that ok?
a: It means the check didn't run: it was skipped, crashed or couldn't find its tools. It told you nothing. NOT_RUN is never a pass; treat it as unfinished until it runs.

q: What is a gate?
a: A gate is the check a project agrees must pass before something counts, like an inspection before a house is signed off. It reports PASS, FAIL or NOT_RUN. Only a PASS makes something QUALIFIED.

q: Isn't it harsh to downgrade an agent's claim?
alt: Why be strict about status words?
a: It isn't a punishment, it's accuracy. Calling something IMPLEMENTED instead of EXERCISED just says what's true. Accurate reports are how people come to trust your work.

q: How do I write a good task for an AI agent?
alt: How do I prompt an agent for a coding task?
a: Four parts: a **goal** in one sentence, **acceptance** written as something you can observe (an exit code, an output, what it prints), a **negative control** that proves your check can fail, and what's **out of scope**. Try `sh examples/start-05-acceptance-criteria/run.sh`.

q: Why isn't 'it works' good enough as acceptance?
a: Because nobody can observe 'it works'. The agent can't tell when it's finished and you can't tell if it succeeded. Name something observable: 'a 12 MB upload exits 1 and prints too large; a 2 MB upload exits 0.'

q: What are acceptance criteria?
a: The conditions the work must meet to be accepted, written before the work starts. A good test: could a stranger read them and tell, without asking you, whether the result passed?

q: Do I need to write code to steer agents well?
alt: Can a non-programmer manage AI agents?
a: No. Clear goals, observable acceptance, a negative control, a scope, and asking for evidence are all things you can do without writing a line of code. That's engineering. Drake's agents track goes further: start with the evidence-first handoff in lesson 8 of that track.
